what to include in a pay range posting
intro: A compliant pay transparency job posting shows a real salary range for the job, in the posting itself. Colorado, for example, requires the rate of compensation or a compensation range, plus a general description of benefits, on each covered posting. This page covers what to include, where the rules apply, what missing ranges cost, and fixes you can make without buying anything.
tldr: Put a real low and high number in the posting body, not in a link or attachment.
Get the range approved and written in one sheet before any posting goes live.
Check each state's law for the place where the job is open, and ask legal about remote roles.
Colorado sets fines of $500 to $10,000 per violation, counted per covered posting.
Many candidates say they would skip a posting with no range, so a blank costs you applicants too.

blocks.text: What a compliant pay range has to show

The core rule is simple. The posting has to show a pay range, or the rate of compensation, in the place the law names. Colorado's rule, as summarized by the National Law Review, asks for the rate of compensation or a compensation range, plus a general description of benefits. Other states and cities write their own wording, so read the rule for each place where you hire.

A range that exists on paper can still fail the test. The range needs real numbers. A phrase such as competitive pay or DOE gives a candidate nothing to compare. Put the low and high figures in the posting text itself, not in a link or an attachment.

items: A low number and a high number, in the same currency and pay period as the offer.
The job title and level the range applies to, so candidates know which role it covers.
The location or locations the range applies to, when pay differs by place.
A short, general note on benefits, such as health coverage, retirement plans and time off.
The same numbers as your sheet and your applicant tracking system, so no one sees a different figure.

blocks.title: Read it as a candidate
blocks.text: Open the draft in the same browser you use for job applications. Find the range without searching the page. If you have to hunt for it, a candidate will too.
Which postings need a range, and where the rules apply

Start with the place where the job is open, then read that state's law for its own definition of coverage. Laws differ on what counts as covered. The sources for this page confirm a few places. Maryland's law took effect October 1, 2024. Indeed Hiring Lab's economist also pointed to California and New York, where pay disclosure laws had been in effect for over a year.

rows: Rate of compensation or a compensation range, plus a general benefits description. Fines of $500 to $10,000 per violation.
Pay disclosure laws in effect for over a year, per Indeed Hiring Lab commentary.
blocks.caption: Confirmed in the sources for this page. Check each agency's own site before you rely on it.

blocks.text: Two situations cause the most confusion. The first is a role that can be filled from more than one state. The second is a posting copied to a new city. In both cases, ask your legal team which rule applies, and write down the answer. Do not assume that a range that works in one place works in the next.
What a missing or vague range costs you

The first cost is legal. In Colorado, fines run from $500 to $10,000 per violation. The count goes by covered posting. A batch of blank ranges is a batch of potential violations, so the exposure grows with every role you publish.

The second cost is candidates. In a Patriot Software survey of 1,000 US adults who applied for a job in the past year, 44% said they are unlikely to apply to a posting with no listed range. That survey came from a payroll software vendor and was not peer reviewed. Read it as a signal, not a rate.

The third cost is trust. The same survey found that 84% believe companies hide pay to reduce workers' negotiating power. A vague range confirms that belief. Candidates then ask for the number on the first call, and the conversation starts from doubt.

The fourth cost is your own time. The research for this page did not turn up a reliable public benchmark for it, so this page does not put a number on it. Keep a simple log for one month instead. Note each range fix, each hiring manager question and each candidate question about pay. That log is your real cost.
Why postings end up without a usable range

Most gaps come from process, not from bad intent. A recruiter wants the posting live. The approved budget arrives late, or it never arrives. The template fills the gap with an old number, or with nothing at all.

items: The budget is approved after the job is already live.
Nobody owns the final number. The hiring manager, the comp partner and the recruiter each assume someone else set it.
The applicant tracking system, the spreadsheet and the offer letter each hold a different range.
The range sits in an attachment or a link, not in the body of the posting.
The benefits note was deleted when someone trimmed the template.

blocks.text: The Colorado rule the sources describe is about the posting itself. A range that surfaces later, in an offer conversation, does not fix the posting.
Pay information in job postings is rising, but more slowly

The trend points up. In September 2024, 57.8% of US postings on Indeed contained some pay information, up from 52.2% a year earlier. Growth is slowing. Indeed Hiring Lab's economist linked the slowdown to large states with disclosure laws that had been in effect for over a year, and to a cooling labor market.

Research on earlier laws points the same way. An NBER working paper found that state disclosure laws raised the share of postings with salary information by 30 percentage points. The paper reports wage increases of 1.3 to 3.6%, and no measured effect on the number of postings. A posting with some pay information is still not automatically compliant, so check your own postings against the rule for each place you hire.
A worked example: fixing one posting from start to finish

Say you are posting a customer success role open to candidates in one state. The hiring manager confirms the budget is open. Start in your shared sheet. Find the row for that role. If there is no row, add one with the title, level, location, low and high numbers, the approver and the date.

Next, open the job template. If your applicant tracking system has a pay transparency feature, check it first. In Greenhouse, a Site Admin creates rules at Configure > Privacy & Compliance. Greenhouse says the feature is on its Core, Plus and Pro tiers, and that Job Admin permissions or higher are needed.

Paste the range into the body of the posting, beside the benefits note. Then open the live post in your browser and read it the way a candidate would. Compare every number with the sheet. If the budget changes later, change the sheet first, then the posting, then tell the hiring manager.
Where Lazur helps, and where it does not

Lazur helps with reading the screen, finding fields and writing the words. It explains what a page says, points at the field you need, guides you through a settings page and drafts a note. It does not decide the range, check the law for you, or click and edit for you. Hold ⌥ ⌘ to ask about anything on screen, and Lazur answers out loud.

Ask how to add a rule in your applicant tracking system. Lazur guides you one click at a time and waits for each click.

Mistakes that keep showing up on live postings

items: Writing DOE or competitive pay where a number belongs.
Starting the range well below the budget the hiring manager approved.
Dropping the benefits note when someone trims the template.
Editing the applicant tracking system but not the sheet, so the next post copies the old number.
Assuming one state's wording covers a role open in another state.

blocks.text: A monthly look at live posts catches most of these early. The check is the cheapest fix on this page, and it works even if you change nothing else.
A one-week routine for compliant posting ranges

Use the week plan below if you have a backlog. It starts with a list, not a rewrite. Keep the approved ranges in one sheet, and add a dropdown for role and location if it helps. The [dropdown list guide](/how-to/create-a-dropdown-list-in-google-sheets) shows the steps for Chrome. The [Google Sheets guide for recruiters](/for/recruiters/google-sheets) covers the tracker, and the [Gmail guide for recruiters](/for/recruiters/gmail) covers approval notes.
Sources and what is still unverified

The numbers on this page come from the sources listed with it. Three gaps remain. The text of the EU Pay Transparency Directive did not open, so this page does not describe EU rules. Colorado's agency guidance did not open, so the penalty range rests on one law firm article. Greenhouse's documentation shows what its feature does, not whether it keeps a company compliant.

faq.question: Does every job posting need a salary range?
faq.answer: No. The rule depends on the place where the job is open, and the sources here cover only a few places in detail. Colorado's rule asks for the rate of compensation or a compensation range, plus a general description of benefits. Check the law for each state and city you hire in, and confirm coverage with your legal team.

faq.question: What counts as a pay range in a job posting?
faq.answer: A low number and a high number, tied to the role and location, shown in the posting text. A phrase such as competitive pay or DOE gives candidates no number to compare. Use real figures in the same currency and pay period as the offer.

faq.question: How much can a missing range cost?
faq.answer: In Colorado, fines run from $500 to $10,000 per violation, and the count is per covered posting that misses a range. Other places set their own penalties, and this page did not verify them. Read the state agency's guidance directly before you rely on any figure.

faq.question: Can I put the range in an attachment or a link instead?
faq.answer: Do not rely on that. The Colorado rule the sources describe is about the posting itself, so put the numbers in the posting text. A link can sit beside the range for extra detail, but it should not be the only place the range appears.

faq.question: Does Greenhouse handle this for me?
faq.answer: Greenhouse offers a pay transparency feature on its Core, Plus and Pro tiers. A Site Admin sets up rules at Configure > Privacy & Compliance, and Job Admins can remove a rule that does not fit a post. Greenhouse also tells users to check local laws with their legal team. The documentation shows what the tool does, not whether it keeps you compliant.

faq.question: What if the budget changes after I post?
faq.answer: Change the sheet first, then the posting, then the applicant tracking rule if you use one. Re-check the live post, not the draft. Tell the hiring manager which number is now the approved range, and date the change.

faq.question: Can Lazur check whether my posting complies?
faq.answer: No. Lazur can read what is on your screen, explain it out loud, point at fields and draft notes. It does not decide what the law requires, and it does not click or edit for you. Confirm the rule with your legal team.

faq.question: Is it safe to share candidate or pay data with an AI tool?
faq.answer: Follow your employer's rules first. Lazur listens and looks at the screen only while you hold the shortcut. Audio and the screenshot go to AI providers to answer and are not stored. Content is never used to train AI models. For regulated roles, check your employer's rules on client or patient data before you share anything.

costs.title: Legal exposure in places like Colorado
costs.text: Colorado's law sets fines of $500 to $10,000 per violation. The count is per covered posting that is missing a compensation range, according to a National Law Review article. A team that posts many roles with blank ranges can accumulate violations quickly. Other states set their own penalties, and this page did not verify them.

costs.title: Candidates who never apply
costs.text: In a Patriot Software survey of 1,000 US adults who applied for a job in the past year, 44% said they are unlikely to apply to a posting with no listed range. The survey comes from a payroll software vendor and was not peer reviewed. Treat it as a directional signal about candidate sentiment, not a rate you can plan around.

costs.title: Trust that is hard to earn back
costs.text: The same survey found 84% believe companies hide pay to reduce workers' negotiating power. A vague range confirms that belief. Candidates then ask for the number on the first call, which starts the conversation from suspicion instead of from the offer.

costs.title: Time spent on fixes and questions
costs.text: No reliable public benchmark for this time cost turned up in the research for this page. Your own log will be more useful than any survey here. For one month, note each range fix, each hiring manager question and each candidate question about pay. That count is your real cost.

causes.title: Pay is set after the posting goes live
causes.text: The budget often gets approved late. The posting goes out with a placeholder, or with no range, and nobody returns to it. A range that was never approved cannot be accurate. Fix this by making the approved range a step before publishing, not a step after.

causes.title: Templates carry old ranges
causes.text: Teams copy a posting from an earlier requisition. The range comes along with it, together with a level, city and budget that no longer match the role. Old numbers look official, so they often get published without a second look.

causes.title: Three systems, three numbers
causes.text: The applicant tracking system, the spreadsheet and the offer letter each hold a range. When the numbers differ, the recruiter tends to use whichever one they see first. Pick one source of truth, and copy from it everywhere.

causes.title: Nobody owns the pay line
causes.text: A hiring manager approves the role. A comp partner approves the band. The recruiter writes the posting. When no one owns the final number, the posting waits, or it goes out without one. Name one owner for the range on every role.

causes.title: Multi-state and remote roles
causes.text: A role that can be filled from more than one place may fall under more than one rule. The sources here do not settle which rule applies to a remote job, and the research for this page excluded remote job guidance. Ask your legal team how they want these roles handled, and write the answer down.

causes.title: Benefits and range sit in different places
causes.text: Some teams keep the pay range in the applicant tracking system but leave the benefits note in a separate document. The posting then looks incomplete to a reader. Keep both in the body text, next to each other.

fixes.title: Build one sheet for every open role
fixes.text: Make a Google Sheets tracker with one row per role. Use columns for role, level, location, low number, high number, approver and date approved. Store it in a shared folder. Ask the comp partner to fill the low and high cells before any role is posted. If a formula confuses you, ask Lazur to explain it on screen.

fixes.title: Get an approved range before you write the posting
fixes.text: Ask the hiring manager and the comp partner for a low and high number. Write both into the sheet with the approver's name and the date. A range without an approver is a guess. Do not publish until the row has both numbers.

fixes.title: Put the range in the body of the posting
fixes.text: Paste the low and high numbers into the main text of the posting, in the same currency and pay period as the offer. Do not leave them only in an attachment, a PDF or a link. Add one sentence that names the level and location the range covers.

fixes.title: Add a general benefits note to every template
fixes.text: Write one short paragraph that describes benefits in general terms, such as health coverage, retirement plans and time off. Keep it inside the template so nobody deletes it by accident. The Colorado rule described in the sources asks for a general description of benefits.

fixes.title: Copy from one source, then check the match
fixes.text: Copy the numbers from the sheet into the applicant tracking system and the posting. Paste them as plain text, then compare all three places. If they differ, the sheet wins, and you correct the other two before publishing.

fixes.title: Read each live post the way a candidate would
fixes.text: Open the live post in your browser, not the draft. Find the range without scrolling far. Check the numbers against the sheet. Repeat the check after every edit, because a draft can look right while the live post is wrong.

fixes.title: Run a monthly check on open roles
fixes.text: Once a month, open the sheet and list every open role. Compare each row with its live post. Note any role missing a range, showing a wrong number or carrying an old level. Give each fix to one named person, with a due date.

plan.label: Day 1
plan.title: List every open role
plan.text: Copy your open roles into one sheet. Add a column for location and a column for the approved range. Mark each role as missing, approved or unclear. You are looking for gaps in this sitting, not fixing them yet.

plan.label: Day 2
plan.title: Request approvals for the gaps
plan.text: Send each hiring manager and comp partner a short note asking for the low and high number. Use a Gmail template so every request reads the same. Schedule a follow-up for any role still missing numbers before you stop for the day.

plan.label: Day 3
plan.title: Rewrite the posting templates
plan.text: Add a range placeholder to the body of the posting template, plus the general benefits paragraph. Replace old ranges with approved numbers. Remove any template that still says DOE or competitive pay.

plan.label: Day 4
plan.title: Fix the live posts
plan.text: Open each live post and update it to match the sheet. Read it as a candidate would, in a private browser window. Log any post you cannot edit, and write down why.

plan.label: Day 5
plan.title: Set the monthly check
plan.text: Create a recurring calendar event for the first working day of each month. Put the sheet link in the event. When it fires, run the list and fix any gaps before the next batch of postings goes out.
